These electrolyzers are described as a hybrid between alkaline and PEM electrolyzers, achieving ramping rates similar to PEM electrolyzers to match renewable electricity generation profiles, but with no critical material requirement, similar to alkaline electrolyzers. Further enhancements to anion-exchange membrane electrolyzer stability and durability are required before these electrolyzers can become cost-competitive with more established hydrogen production methods (Rouwenhorst 2023; Mulk et al. 2024). Extracting geologic hydrogen (i.e., hydrogen naturally produced in the Earth’s subsurface) has garnered significant attention in 2024 and 2025 as a high-risk, high-reward hydrogen production method (Pare 2024; Bettenhausen 2025; Currie 2025). It is high risk because it is unknown whether hydrogen in the subsurface could be extracted at high enough concentrations and quantities to be economic over a typical production project lifetime. It is high reward because if it were to be found in high concentrations with meaningful supply levels, it would be cost- competitive with conventional fossil-based hydrogen production methods and have fewer air quality impacts (Blackford 2024; Gelman et al. 2025; Hasiuk and Conley 2025). As of 2023, roughly 40 companies were in search of economic natural hydrogen deposits ranging from startups to major oil and gas companies (Meredith 2025; Hasiuk and Conley 2025). The primary mechanisms scientists believe geologic hydrogen is produced from include serpentinization and radiolysis (Gaucher 2020; Gelman et al. 2025). Serpentinization occurs when water is reduced by the oxidation of iron-containing minerals (i.e., oxygen is stripped from the water molecule, leaving H ). Hydrogen production via radiolysis occurs when ionizing 2 radiation from uranium, thorium, and other radioactive elements in the subsurface split water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen (Gaucher 2020; Hasiuk and Conley 2025). Figure 33, which is from the U.S. Geological Survey, shows the prospective locations for geologic hydrogen in the contiguous United States (Gelman et al. 2025). The U.S. Geological Survey estimates that the most probable global supply of geologic hydrogen is around 5.6 trillion metric tons.
